name: Negativland
label: SST
lede: Two Concord teenagers with tape machines grew into the collective that invented "culture jamming," faked a murder link for publicity, got sued by U2's label and their own, and mailed a founder's ashes out with a CD.

eras.title: Tape decks in the suburbs
eras.text: Negativland began as two high school kids in Concord, California, cutting up sound in their bedrooms, named after a Neu! song. A Berkeley late-night radio slot turned them from a home-taping project into a broadcast one, and gave the world a phrase.

years.h: Mark Hosler and Richard Lyons start Negativland
years.p: Two Concord high school students name the group after a song by German krautrock band Neu!; their label, Seeland, is named after a Neu! '75 track.

years.h: Negativland: 15,000 hand-made covers
years.p: The debut came in hand-made, numbered sleeves. The band says it made 15,000 unique covers over 15 years: 9,000 for vinyl, 6,000 for CD.

years.cap: Don Joyce on Over the Edge, KPFA
years.h: Over the Edge hits KPFA at midnight
years.p: [[Don Joyce|86a06391-4973-4f1b-a02e-95fe192dc977]] starts the show on Berkeley's KPFA, Sundays at midnight after Music from the Hearts of Space. He hosts it for over 30 years.
years.xp: Callers phoned in unscreened sounds, rants and performances, which Joyce mixed live with old radio, ads and his Booper, a circuit-bent oscillator. The Internet Archive holds more than 1,300 episodes.

years.h: A Big 10-8 Place on Seeland
years.p: The third album, released on the band's own Seeland label.

years.h: Don Joyce coins "culture jamming"
years.p: On Over the Edge Vol. 1: JAMCON'84, Joyce's alter ego Crosley Bendix calls the whole world the culture jammer's studio.

eras.title: A fire, an SST deal, and a fake murder link
eras.text: Negativland's best-known record nearly burned before it came out. When SST wanted them to tour it, they invented a reason not to, and the media ran with it.

years.h: Fire wrecks the El Cerrito studio
years.p: Negativland's El Cerrito studio burns. The band saves the master tapes and rushes to Los Angeles to confirm the album with SST.

years.h: Escape from Noise on SST, with Jerry Garcia
years.p: The first Negativland record on an established indie. Guests include [[Jerry Garcia|1ecff755-607d-4130-9a8a-8873f27e5de5]], Mickey Hart, [[Jello Biafra|2280ca0e-6968-4349-8c36-cb0cbd6ee95f]], [[Mark Mothersbaugh|6ff5f720-9fcd-434c-8a62-dc9dd123bde7]], [[Fred Frith|4801bad4-1b42-4c9e-84b1-bf61067ab67c]], [[Henry Kaiser|3b4ce4be-55a1-44bb-abdc-bcc504f30ca1]] and [[The Residents|8c9b336e-acc8-4e20-9195-6ed0634da9fc]].
years.xp: Christianity Is Stupid is built on sermon samples from evangelist Estus Pirkle's 1968 LP If Footmen Tire You, What Will Horses Do?. Early copies of the album came with a yellow Car Bomb bumper sticker.

years.h: The hoax: a made-up federal agent and David Brom
years.p: To get out of an SST tour, Negativland issues a press release claiming federal official "Dick Jordan" asked them not to leave town: Christianity Is Stupid might have inspired David Brom, who killed his family in Rochester, Minnesota.
years.xp:
Neither Dick Jordan nor the band's quoted attorney, "Hal Stakke," existed, and Brom reportedly owned no Negativland music. Most journalists were skeptical; San Francisco's KPIX ran it as news anyway.

The Village Voice ran two paragraphs, noting the vagueness might mean it was just publicity.

years.h: Helter Stupid turns the hoax into an album
years.p: Side one takes apart the Brom story and the news coverage it got. Side two is eight versions of The Perfect Cut, built from a 1977 radio production.

eras.title: The letter U and the numeral 2
eras.text: A parody single aimed at U2 fans turned into two lawsuits, one from U2's label and one from Negativland's own. The band lost the record and its label and came out as the loudest artists in America on fair use.

years.h: U2: Casey Kasem outtakes and a U2 parody
years.p: Two takes on I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For, laced with bootlegged outtakes of [[Casey Kasem|9dd99129-8069-4528-b10d-5ca0179e42eb]] swearing. The sleeve prints "U2" far bigger than "Negativland."

years.src: Westword · The New Republic · Far Out
years.h: Island Records sues over the U2 EP
years.p: Island and Warner Chappell say the single is meant to confuse fans waiting for Achtung Baby. SST agrees to destroy remaining copies and, per Westword, pay about $90,000 in legal costs.
years.xp: Greg Ginn's first response, per The New Republic, was that SST was putting it out anyway. Then SST settled and announced it would recoup its losses from Negativland. The band replaced the single with Guns, dedicated to their favorite Irish rock band, its label and its attorneys.

years.h: Negativland vs. Greg Ginn
years.p: Negativland prints SST's financial documents in its magazine The Letter U and the Numeral 2, calls the label hypocrites and leaves. [[Greg Ginn|4f35de64-27ab-4426-95fd-8d454cda4e48]] answers with a press release and a breach-of-contract suit.
years.xp: Ginn told Westword the band wanted to skate off without meeting its obligations. In the final settlement Westword reported, Negativland got four SST albums back and Ginn got over $30,000 plus a live album.

q: There's at least six records out there that are direct samples from our stuff.
years.h: Posing as journalists, they interview The Edge
years.p: Through Mondo 2000 publisher R. U. Sirius, Mark Hosler and Don Joyce interview U2's The Edge, then reveal who they are and grill him on sampling.

years.h: Fair Use: the lawsuit as a 270-page book
years.p: Negativland's book-and-CD tells the whole U2 and SST saga, with an appendix of essays on copyright, on Seeland.

years.h: Sonic Outlaws puts them on film
years.p: Craig Baldwin's documentary on culture jamming features Negativland and the U2 case.

eras.title: Pepsi, Chumbawamba and a robot Lincoln
eras.text: Free of SST, Negativland aimed at soda, radio conglomerates and copyright law itself, and started building gallery shows out of its own junk.

years.h: Dispepsi: afraid to print its own title
years.p: The Pepsi-ad collage hid its name in anagrams in case of a lawsuit. Once Pepsi's lawyers said they wouldn't sue, the band started calling it Dispepsi.

years.h: SST releases a live album the band didn't want
years.p: Greg Ginn's SST puts out Negativ(e)land: Live on Tour against Negativland's wishes.

years.h: The ABCs of Anarchism with Chumbawamba
years.p: An EP with [[Chumbawamba|7b7b1e6f-e73e-41a0-9d72-8f0b30c6992d]] built on Alexander Berkman's writing, Tubthumping, the Teletubbies theme and Anarchy in the UK.

years.h: Pirate radio hits the broadcasters' convention
years.p: A Negativland parody of Clear Channel stations goes out on pirate radio during the National Association of Broadcasters meeting in Seattle.

years.h: Helping write the Creative Commons Sampling License
years.p: The band that got sued over samples helps draft the license meant to make sampling legal.

years.h: Negativlandland and an animatronic Lincoln
years.p: A 25th-anniversary art show at Gigantic Artspace, 59 Franklin Street in Manhattan, with a robot Abraham Lincoln and a hands-on Booper built by [[David Wills|b57a41a4-7741-4ef3-9071-81d35217d681]], "the Weatherman."

eras.title: Ashes in the mail
eras.text: A new member arrived and then, within 16 months, three longtime members died. Negativland kept going and turned Don Joyce's death into a record in the most Negativland way possible.

years.h: Jon Leidecker, a.k.a. Wobbly, joins
years.p: [[Jon Leidecker|54ebe373-8d62-44f0-a0bd-d306d6681dc5]] becomes a member; after Don Joyce's death he takes over Over the Edge with Robert Cole.

years.h: Rivers Cuomo releases his song called Negativland
years.p: [[Rivers Cuomo|87b6344f-c874-49ce-a8b3-e467ed6e05d0]] wrote it in 1993; it finally comes out on Alone III: The Pinkerton Years.

years.h: It's All in Your Head, packaged in a Bible
years.p: The album about monotheism comes inside a King James Bible.

years.h: Ian Allen dies at 56
years.p: The former member dies of complications from heart valve surgery.

years.h: Don Joyce dies of heart failure at 71
years.p: Joyce, host of Over the Edge for more than 30 years and the man who named culture jamming, dies in Oakland.

years.h: Co-founder Richard Lyons dies at 57
years.p: Lyons dies of complications from nodular melanoma at a nursing facility.

years.h: Don Joyce's ashes ship with The Chopping Channel
years.p: The first 1,000 CDs of Over the Edge Vol. 9: The Chopping Channel each include two grams of Joyce's cremated remains, plus 750 of his audio carts.
years.xp: The packaging got wide attention online. Ryan Worsley later made How Radio Isn't Done, an 80-minute film with archival footage of Joyce.

years.h: True False, back to something like songs
years.p: A double album and a return to song structures, with Ian Allen heard via archival recordings.

years.h: The World Will Decide
years.p: An album about surveillance and digital identity.

sources.title: The New Republic via Bunk History: The Unraveling of SST Records
Far Out: The record that U2 sued out of existence
